To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the amplitude of CCF of dense samples is a fingerprint of their ordering, while the coherence of the probing beam is crucial in determining the CCF shape.
the cross-correlation of the scattered intensity from a sample of scattering objects is a function of the transverse coherence, of the size of the scattering object and of the symmetry of the object.

(a) the cross correlation function is a fingerprint of local order in the sample, (b) the amplitude of the cross-correlation is a fingerprint of ordering in the sample, and (c) in the case of dense samples the cross-correlation of partially coherent beams is the same as the cross-correlation from an isolated object.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the CCF of two-dimensional dense monoisperse systems, and its relation to the sample’s symmetry and degree of order.
the role of the coherence of the probing beam in the CCF analysis of dense two-dimensional systems.
understanding the role of the coherence of the probe in the analysis of diffraction pattern from dense systems and the possibility to retrieve structural information at a sub-particle level.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in a sample with a high degree of ordering, at partial coherence the CCF corresponds to the CCF of an individual scattering particle, and at complete coherence the CCF is the convolution of the CCF of the scattering particle and the CCF of its environment.
the CCF of dense mono-disperse samples at full beam coherence is a function of the sample symmetry, whereas at partial coherence it becomes a function of the individual scattering object.
the CCF of dense samples is a fingerprint of both the symmetry and the ordering in the system, which is robust against the partial coherence of the probing beam.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CCF is an effective tool to probe the symmetry and the local order of dense systems at different size scale.

the CCF analysis is a powerful tool to investigate the static and dynamic structure of dense systems at the atomic scale, and that the coherence of the probing beam is crucial in the formation of a diffraction pattern and in the analysis of the CCF.
the transverse coherence can be used as a knob to tune the sensitivity of the CCF analysis to the local structure of a sample.
